verdicts.trueWording: "Its internal focalization is immersive and often pronounced"
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (698 KB, 143 pp.) extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on printed p.125 (PDF p.127): "Robin Hobb's (1952-) Ship of Magic (1998) is a pure figural narrative formally similar to Martin's. Its internal focalization is immersive and often pronounced, and its strong figurality is on a par with the figurality in Martin and Donaldson." Both limbs (Lagus; Ship of Magic) supported. Metadata nit: p.125 falls in ch. 4 (4.3 'From the 1980s to the 2000s: Toward Figural Fantasy', pp.116-131), not ch. 5 (Conclusion, p.134) as the claim's page field says. Author/venue confirmed on the title page: Timo Lagus, Master's Thesis, Department of English, University of Helsinki, 5 December 2006.

verdicts.trueWording: "Sitting by her dying husband's bedside, Ronica Vestrit, the matriarch"
verdicts.note: Verbatim (curly apostrophe) on printed p.127: "Sitting by her dying husband's bedside, Ronica Vestrit, the matriarch of a once-powerful Liveship trader family from Bingtown, reflects on her grief, her husband, and the maid Rache in Hobb's Ship of Magic:" followed by a block quotation (pp.127-128, cited '(50-51)'). Every limb holds: the exemplification frame is Lagus's own sentence on p.125 -- "The following excerpts exemplify the characteristic figural perspectivism in the three novels"; the reprinted passage has Ronica weighing whether to send Rache back to Davad, and the text names her status -- "While she remained in Bingtown, she was nominally an indentured servant." Metadata nit: the passage begins on p.127 and runs to p.128 (ch. 4), not pp.126-127 / ch. 5.

verdicts.trueWording: "that of a historian getting distracted by their own role"
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (1.5 MB, 151 pp.) extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on printed p.56: "The narrator version of Fitz inevitably ends up focusing on the big-picture repercussions of his existence: as a narrator, Fitz's perspective is that of a historian getting distracted by their own role in the history." 'Older narrating Fitz' is supported -- the thesis uses 'older/narrator-Fitz' at p.92. TWO metadata errors, neither a limb of the claim sentence: (1) the thesis title page reads 'Caitlyn Moon', not 'Emily Moon' (title, degree, Kent and October 2024 all otherwise confirmed); (2) the quote is on p.56 in Chapter One ('Wit and Skill', p27-63), not ch. 2 p.55.

verdicts.trueWording: "the abrupt addition and disappearance of quotation marks"
verdicts.note: Verbatim on printed p.92: "The dichotomy between the comfortable use of she/her pronouns versus the abrupt addition and disappearance of quotation marks around the pronoun demonstrates a difference between the automatic acceptance of a child versus the learnt disdain of an adult." The 'seam' limb is supported by the immediately preceding sentence: "the first half of the quote could easily be read as from the young Fitz ... whereas the second quote more clearly comes from the older/narrator-Fitz"; the marked pronoun is Chade-as-Lady-Thyme's "'She'." Metadata: p.92, not p.88; and the author is Caitlyn Moon, not Emily Moon.

verdicts.trueWording: "casts the fantastic as an unquestioned, familiar aspect of the setting"
verdicts.note: Fetched the article wikitext raw (action=raw, 52 KB). Style section, verbatim: "Hobb uses a style within the fantasy genre that casts the fantastic as an unquestioned, familiar aspect of the setting: this creates an 'illusion of familiarity' for the reader, according to scholar Susan Mandala." Cited {{sfnp|Mandala|2010|pp=100-102}}, matching the claim's source line exactly. Both limbs (the framing; the illusion of familiarity) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "the narration matches how he experiences the dream"
verdicts.note: Style section, verbatim: "When Fitz first shares a dream with a dog, the narration matches how he experiences the dream - as a perfectly natural, as opposed to fantastic, event - through language that is 'lexically coherent' across the human and animal segments, in Mandala's view." The 'lexically coherent across the human and the animal parts' limb is on the page word for word as 'across the human and animal segments'; cited {{sfnp|Mandala|2010|p=102}} plus Larsson 2021 pp.130-131 (claim's source line says Mandala 101-102; the article gives p.102 here and pp.101-102 for the adjacent Skill sentence).

verdicts.trueWording: "the narrative does not address the term directly"
verdicts.note: Style section, verbatim: "Similarly, when Fitz first mentions the telepathic Skill, the narrative does not address the term directly, assuming that its meaning is known in-world, but instead focuses on the Skill's potential effect on Fitz's memory, and its addictive qualities." Both limbs supported -- 'does not explain the term' = 'does not address the term directly'; 'treating its meaning as known inside the world' = 'assuming that its meaning is known in-world'. Cited {{sfnp|Mandala|2010|pp=101-102}}.

verdicts.trueWording: "Fitz describes his immediate family in the same terms as the"
verdicts.note: Style section, verbatim: "For instance, Fitz describes his immediate family in the same terms as the strangers he meets: his grandfather becomes 'the tall man', and his mother is 'a voice' that is distant and unfamiliar, signifying his emotional distance from them." Both named details ('the tall man', 'a voice') present; attributed on the page to Mandala, cited {{sfnp|Mandala|2010|pp=128-130}}, matching the claim's source line.

verdicts.trueWording: "short memoirs prefacing each chapter that narrate a fictional history"
verdicts.note: Style section, verbatim: "The novels contain short memoirs prefacing each chapter that narrate a fictional history of the setting: these excerpts are also unreliable narratives, relaying 'recollection and gossip'." Both limbs supported. The claim correctly attributes this to the Wikipedia article as such; on the page it carries {{sfnp|Mendlesohn|2014|p=16}}.

verdicts.trueWording: "the all-too-human factors of avarice and pettiness"
verdicts.note: Fetched the live page (205 KB HTML, 200) and stripped tags. Section 'The Typical Sites of Memory: The Stone Quarry, the Dragon Garden, and Kelsingra', verbatim: "Attention to such concerns-the all-too-human factors of avarice and pettiness-is a hallmark of Hobb's writing". The looting limb is supported two sentences earlier: "Kelsingra, and presumably the quarry and garden with which they are linked, end up subject to looting-not only by FitzChivalry ... but also by avaricious merchants." Kelsingra is a memorial city on the page: "That city is itself a silent memorial of a bygone civilization" and "serving as a necropolis".

verdicts.trueWording: "a multi-generational loan, secured by potential marriages, to purchase one"
verdicts.note: Section 'The Strange Sites of Memory: The Liveships', verbatim: "As such, they are highly prized-such that a multi-generational loan, secured by potential marriages, to purchase one is not at all uncommon-and, in some ways, are regarded as both enduring members of their owning families and the defining emblems of those same families." Bingtown limb supported ('Peculiar to the Bingtown Traders'), family limb supported ('owning families'). One wording nit that does not change the grade: the page says 'is not at all uncommon' (litotes), which the claim renders as 'commonly takes'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Elliott presents this as how Hobb *introduces* Kelsingra, i.e. through Fitz's non-perception
verdicts.trueWording: "When FitzChivalry first encounters Kelsingra, he finds it empty"
verdicts.note: The quotation is on the page word for word: "When FitzChivalry first encounters Kelsingra, he finds it empty, perceiving no signs of life around him;". But Elliott makes no claim about Hobb's technique of introduction, and the same sentence continues into positive perception, not absence: "as he searches it, he finds that 'Whole domes of roofs had fallen in...outer walls had fallen away entirely' ... and sees, among others, 'the tatters of ancient hangings, a collapsed wooden bench.'" Elliott also introduces Kelsingra two sentences earlier in his own descriptive voice ('That city is itself a silent memorial of a bygone civilization'), and later notes the city 'replays' its memories to Fitz, 'immersing him in images of the daily lives of inhabitants' -- so the city is not rendered through what Fitz fails to perceive. Grade is PARTIAL, not VERIFIED: the narrative-craft limb is the claim's gloss, not Elliott's.

Fetched the PLOS article page (224 KB HTML, 200) and stripped tags -- full text present. Verbatim in the Introduction: "the results will be presented and discussed for the forty-seven best-selling books in terms of typical network measures" (and Methods: 'We have arbitrarily restricted our analysis to forty-seven books'). The Hobb limb is verbatim in the same section's corpus list: "the three 'Liveship Traders' [25-27] and four 'Rain Wild Chronicles' [28-31] books by Robin Hobb", and the reference list carries exactly seven Hobb titles (Ship of Magic, The Mad Ship, Ship of Destiny, The Dragon Keeper, Dragon Haven, City of Dragons, Blood of Dragons). Nit: the 47 also include Les Miserables, which the paper itself calls 'one classic' rather than a best-seller.

verdicts.trueWording: "relevant in the identification of the author's style like the dialog"
verdicts.note: Verbatim under the heading 'Conclusion and future work' (curly apostrophe in 'author's'): "Finally, some features were identified that might be relevant in the identification of the author's style like the dialog spacing and alias network topology." Both named features and the hedge ('might be relevant' -> 'may identify') are supported, and the section field matches the page's own heading.

verdicts.trueWording: "The dendrogram shows a good clustering of certain series"
verdicts.note: Verbatim in Results, immediately after 'Fig 21. Dendrogram for the hierarchical clustering of the books using the Ward variance minimization algorithm.': "The dendrogram shows a good clustering of certain series: 'Harry Potter', 'The Rain Wild Chronicles', 'The Lunar Chronicles' and 'The Mortal Instruments', for instance, appear to be clustered. Other series are more scattered, which can be attributed to a fluctuation of style: for instance, 'The Wheel of Time' is separated in three sub-clusters." Rain Wild limb explicit. The 'absence of style fluctuation' limb rests on the authors' own two-sentence contrast (scattered = fluctuation of style, Wheel of Time named) rather than on a separate positive sentence -- close enough to stand, and the paper says nothing to the contrary.
